title: Power of Three
description: Brute force to optimized: dividing by three in a loop versus a fixed-constant divisibility trick, plus a logarithm alternative.

blocks.text: Given a number n, decide whether it is a power of three, meaning it can be written as 3 raised to some non-negative whole number exponent, like 1, 3, 9, 27, and so on.

blocks.title: Analogy: A Cell That Always Splits Into Three
blocks.text: Picture a single cell that, once per generation, splits into exactly three new cells, and every one of those does the same thing next generation. A population size is only reachable under this rule if it can be traced back through whole generations of tripling, starting from a single cell. A population of 27 fits perfectly (three generations of tripling). A population of 20 could never appear, no matter how many generations pass, since tripling alone can never land exactly on it.

blocks.caption: A power of three divides evenly by 3, all the way down to 1

blocks.content: {"headers":["n","Divide by 3 chain","Power of three?","Why"],"rows":[["27","27 to 9 to 3 to 1","Yes, 3 to the power 3","Every division lands cleanly with no remainder, all the way down to 1."]]}

{"headers":["n","Divide by 3 chain","Power of three?","Why"],"rows":[["45","45 to 15 to 5, then 5 does not divide evenly by 3","No","The chain breaks the moment a division leaves a remainder, proving it was never built from pure tripling."]]}

blocks.text: 1 is 3 raised to the power 0, so it counts as a power of three trivially, with no division needed at all.
Before writing any code, it helps to reason about what makes powers of three different from powers of two here.

blocks.title: How Should We Think?
blocks.text:
Observation 1: Tripling a single starting unit again and again, 1, 3, 9, 27, always produces a number that divides evenly by 3, over and over, all the way down to 1.

Observation 2: Powers of three have no clean single-bit shape in binary the way powers of two do, since 3 is not a power of the number base computers use internally, so a bit trick like the power of two problem's does not directly apply here.

Observation 3: Instead of checking bits, a power of three can be checked against a known, fixed reference: the largest power of three that fits in a normal 32 bit integer, since every smaller power of three divides evenly into it, and nothing else does.

Observation 4: That fixed reference turns a repeated division loop into one single divisibility check against a constant.
That reasoning alone already sketches the shortcut: no bit trick exists here, but a fixed numeric reference point works just as well.
The most direct approach is to repeatedly divide n by 3, the same tripling process from the analogy but run in reverse. If n ever fails to divide evenly, it could not have come from pure tripling.

items: If n is less than 1, return false immediately.
While n is greater than 1, check whether it is evenly divisible by 3.
If not divisible, return false.
Otherwise divide n by 3 and repeat.
If the loop reaches exactly 1, return true.

blocks.caption: Brute force flow: keep dividing by 3 and check for a clean division every time

blocks.text: Why the code is written this way

items: The n < 1 check happens before the loop, as a dedicated early rejection, since the loop's own division logic has no way to naturally reject zero or negative numbers on its own.
The divisibility check happens before dividing, not after, since dividing an already-non-divisible number would silently discard the remainder that proves the chain is broken.
The loop condition is n > 1, not n > 0, specifically so the loop stops exactly when n has been fully reduced to 1 by clean division, which is the success condition.

blocks.text: This works because a power of three, by definition, can be divided by 3 repeatedly with no remainder until only 1 is left. Any number that fails to divide evenly along the way could not have been built purely by tripling.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(log base 3 of n), since n shrinks by a factor of 3 every iteration.
Space: O(1).

Limitation: unlike powers of two, powers of three have no simple single-bit pattern to check directly, since 3 is not a power of the number base computers use internally. There is still a useful shortcut though: every power of three divides evenly into any larger power of three, since 3 to the power a is a factor of 3 to the power b whenever a is less than or equal to b.

blocks.title: The Optimization Journey
blocks.text:
Why looping and dividing works but is not necessary: it rediscovers, one division at a time, something that can be checked all at once against a fixed known value.

What makes a fixed reference possible here: 32 bit integers have a hard upper limit, so there is exactly one largest power of three that still fits, 3 to the power 19.

Why does every smaller power of three divide evenly into that largest one: because 3 to the power a is always a factor of 3 to the power b whenever a is less than or equal to b, a basic property of exponents sharing the same base.

Does the reverse hold, that only powers of three divide evenly into it: yes, since 1162261467 factors purely into 3s, nothing else can divide it evenly.

The core idea: check whether 1162261467 mod n equals 0, no loop, no repeated division.

3 to the power 19 (1162261467) is the largest power of three that fits inside a standard 32 bit integer, since 3 to the power 20 would overflow it. Every smaller power of three, and only powers of three, divide evenly into this one fixed number.
The optimization is to check divisibility against this single fixed constant, instead of looping through repeated division.
If n is positive, check whether 1162261467 (3 to the power 19) is evenly divisible by n. If it is, n must itself be a power of three.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Step","Computation","Value","Why"],"rows":[["1","1162261467 mod 27","0","A remainder of 0 means 27 divides evenly into the fixed largest power of three."],["2","Remainder is 0","True, power of three","Only a pure power of three can divide evenly into a number built entirely from factors of 3."]]}

blocks.caption: Optimized flow: one division against a fixed constant replaces the entire loop

blocks.text: This works because 1162261467 is exactly 3 to the power 19, and its only prime factorization is 3 multiplied by itself 19 times. Any number that divides 1162261467 evenly, with no remainder, must therefore also be built purely from factors of 3, meaning it must itself be some smaller power of three, 3 to the power 0 through 3 to the power 19. Any number that is not a pure power of three, like 45, which factors as 9 times 5, will always leave a nonzero remainder, since the factor of 5 has nowhere to go.

items: The constant 1162261467 is computed once, ahead of time, as 3 to the power 19, specifically because it is the largest power of three that still fits inside a standard 32 bit signed integer.
The n <= 0 check still comes first, exactly as in the brute force, since the divisibility trick alone has no built-in way to reject zero or negative inputs.
The entire check is a single modulo operation against that fixed constant, no loop, no repeated division of n itself.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(1), a single modulo operation, regardless of how large n is.
Space: O(1).
10. Further Optimization: The Logarithm Approach (With a Caution)

A different, also constant time idea is to take the logarithm of n in base 3. If n truly is a power of three, that logarithm should come out to a whole number. This alone is not safe to trust, floating point logarithms can be very slightly off from the true value, so the result must always be rounded and then verified exactly by raising 3 back to that power and comparing it to n.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Step","Computation","Value","Why"],"rows":[["1","log of 27 base 3","approximately 3.0","Floating point logarithms can land very slightly off from an exact whole number."],["2","Rounded to nearest whole number","3","Rounding turns the approximate result into a candidate integer exponent."],["3","3 raised to the power 3","27","Raising 3 back to that candidate exponent recomputes an exact integer to check against."],["4","Equals original n","True, power of three","This exact comparison is the mandatory verification step, never trust the log alone."]]}

blocks.caption: Further optimization: estimate with logarithms, then verify exactly

items: Taking the log of n in base 3 estimates the exponent using floating point division of natural logarithms, which is inherently an approximation, not an exact integer computation.
Rounding that estimate to the nearest whole number is what turns a possibly slightly-off floating point value into a candidate integer exponent worth testing.

Raising 3 back to that rounded power and comparing it exactly to n is the mandatory verification step, since trusting the logarithm alone, without this check, is exactly the kind of subtle bug that can silently produce wrong answers near the edges of floating point precision.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(1), identical to the fixed constant approach.
Space: O(1). This is a stylistic alternative, not a complexity improvement, and it is genuinely riskier: skipping the verification step, as some incorrect solutions do, can silently produce wrong answers near the edges of floating point precision.

blocks.text: The core pattern here is using a known, fixed reference point (the largest power of three that fits in the integer range) to turn a repeated division into a single check. It is also a good reminder that clever tricks involving floating point math, like the logarithm approach, need an exact verification step to be trustworthy.

items: Trusting a logarithm based check without verifying the rounded result exactly, which can silently produce wrong answers.
Forgetting that n = 1 is a valid power of three (3 to the power 0), not a special case to reject.
Hardcoding the wrong constant for the largest representable power of three, always double check it against the integer type's actual range.

blocks.text: This problem is a good test of whether a candidate can adapt bit-trick style thinking (from problems like Power of Two) to a base that does not have a clean binary shortcut. Proposing the largest-power-in-range trick, and being explicit about why the logarithm approach needs a verification step, shows real numerical care.

blocks.title: If The Interviewer Says This, Think This
blocks.text:
If the interviewer says "can you do this without a loop", think: check divisibility against the largest power of three that fits the integer type.
If the interviewer says "can you use logarithms", think: yes, but only with an exact verification step afterward, never trust the rounded log alone.
If the interviewer says "why doesn't the power of two bit trick work here", think: 3 is not a power of the binary base, so there is no equivalent single-bit shape to check.

items: Why does a power of two have a simple bit trick but a power of three does not?
How would you find the exact value of the largest power of three that fits a given integer type, without hardcoding it?
Why is verifying the logarithm approach's result mandatory rather than optional?
Can you generalize the fixed constant divisibility trick to check for a power of any fixed base?
What would change if n could be a very large number represented as a string, too big for a normal integer type?
"Is this a power of k" problems for other bases, which reuse either the fixed-largest-constant trick or the logarithm-plus-verification approach.
The power of two problem, which solves the same shape of question with a bit trick specifically because 2 is the computer's own base, a useful contrast for why that trick does not generalize.
Floating point precision pitfalls in general, where any result derived from log, sqrt, or similar functions needs an exact integer verification step before being trusted.
Divisibility based checks that reuse a single precomputed constant instead of looping, a pattern that also shows up in problems checking for factors, multiples, or coprimality against a fixed bound.

blocks.title: Complexity Summary
blocks.text: The brute force loop runs in O(log n) time and O(1) space. Both the fixed constant approach and the logarithm approach run in O(1) time and O(1) space, a genuine complexity class improvement, with the fixed constant approach being the safer of the two since it avoids floating point precision risk entirely.

items: Pattern: using a known, fixed reference point, the largest power of three that fits the integer type, to turn a repeated division into a single divisibility check.
Core Idea: 1162261467, 3 to the power 19, is built purely from factors of 3, so a number divides it evenly if and only if that number is itself some smaller power of three.
Time: O(log base 3 of n) for the brute force loop, O(1) for both the fixed constant and logarithm approaches.
Space: O(1) across every version.

Most Important Observation: powers of three have no clean bit level shortcut the way powers of two do, so the key insight here is a fixed numeric reference point rather than a bitwise trick, and any floating point shortcut, like logarithms, needs an exact verification step to be trustworthy.
Interview Difficulty: easy to get a correct loop based answer, but proposing the constant-divisibility trick, and being careful about the logarithm approach's precision risk, is what stands out.
One line memory trick: does the biggest power of three that fits divide n evenly?
